common_name: America Grape (T.V. Munson-Bred Pierce's Disease-Resistant Texas Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings in early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; bred by Texas grape pioneer T.V. Munson in Denison from the native American species Vitis lincecumii and Vitis rupestris, giving it strong resistance to Pierce's disease without any Vitis labrusca or vinifera parentage.

directions: Bred in the late 1800s by T.V. Munson of Denison, Texas, America was selected specifically because its wild American parentage kept it healthy where European and labrusca-type vines succumbed to Pierce's disease and major fungal diseases. The blue-black berries are tart and better suited to juice, jelly, and home winemaking than fresh eating, and the vigorous vine still survives today largely through heirloom grape collections and Texas viticulture history programs rather than commercial vineyards. Grow on a strong trellis in full sun and prune hard each winter, since the vine can be quite vigorous once established.
sources: Grayson College — T.V. Munson Memorial Vineyard and Viticulture Program

common_name: Camminare Noir Grape (UC Davis Pierce's Disease-Resistant Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring on a cordon trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; bred by Dr. Andy Walker at UC Davis using marker-assisted selection to introgress Pierce's disease resistance from the wild species Vitis arizonica into a predominantly vinifera background.

directions: Released by UC Davis in 2019, Camminare Noir carries Pierce's disease resistance from the wild Southwestern species Vitis arizonica bred back into a mostly Vitis vinifera vine, giving growers in high-PD-pressure regions like the Texas Gulf Coast a red wine grape with far better survival odds than traditional European varieties. The wine has been compared to a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Petite Sirah, with good color and structure, and it has already been planted experimentally in several Texas vineyards battling severe sharpshooter-driven Pierce's disease pressure. Train on a cordon trellis and prune in late winter; because the variety is still new to commercial production, availability through licensed nurseries remains limited.
sources: UC Davis College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences

common_name: Paseante Noir Grape (UC Davis Pierce's Disease-Resistant Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring on a cordon trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; bred by Dr. Andy Walker at UC Davis to carry Pierce's disease resistance from Vitis arizonica into a mostly vinifera vine suited to hot, humid, high-disease-pressure regions.

directions: One of five Pierce's disease-resistant wine grapes released by UC Davis in 2019, Paseante Noir was bred by Dr. Andy Walker using marker-assisted selection to move resistance from the wild Vitis arizonica into a predominantly vinifera vine. The resulting wine is described as similar in style to Zinfandel, with good fruit character despite the vine's mostly-wild disease-resistance parentage. Gulf South and Texas growers facing severe glassy-winged sharpshooter and Pierce's disease pressure are beginning to trial it as an alternative to susceptible European varieties. Train on a cordon trellis in full sun and expect limited nursery availability while the variety is still being multiplied commercially.
sources: UC Davis College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences

common_name: Errante Noir Grape (UC Davis Pierce's Disease-Resistant Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring on a cordon trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; bred by Dr. Andy Walker at UC Davis to carry Pierce's disease resistance from Vitis arizonica into a predominantly vinifera red wine grape.

directions: Errante Noir is one of the UC Davis Pierce's disease-resistant wine grape releases from Dr. Andy Walker's breeding program, which used marker-assisted selection to introgress resistance from the wild Vitis arizonica while keeping the vine predominantly Vitis vinifera. The wine has been compared most closely to Cabernet Sauvignon in style. Because the resistance trait allows the vine to tolerate the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa spread by sharpshooters, it is of particular interest to Gulf Coast and Texas growers where Pierce's disease historically eliminates most European wine grapes. Train on a cordon trellis in full sun and expect limited nursery supply as commercial propagation ramps up.
sources: UC Davis College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences

common_name: Ambulo Blanc Grape (UC Davis Pierce's Disease-Resistant White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring on a cordon trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; bred by Dr. Andy Walker at UC Davis to carry Pierce's disease resistance from Vitis arizonica into a predominantly vinifera white wine grape.

directions: Released by UC Davis in 2019 as one of the first Pierce's disease-resistant wine grapes bred through marker-assisted selection, Ambulo Blanc carries resistance from the wild Southwestern species Vitis arizonica while remaining predominantly Vitis vinifera. The resulting wine is described as similar to Sauvignon Blanc, offering a genuine vinifera-style white option for regions where Pierce's disease has long ruled out European varieties. Texas Gulf Coast vineyards facing high sharpshooter pressure are among the early adopters trialing the variety. Train on a cordon trellis in full sun; supply through licensed nurseries remains limited while multiplication continues.
sources: UC Davis College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences

common_name: Caminante Blanc Grape (UC Davis Pierce's Disease-Resistant White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring on a cordon trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; released in late 2019 by UC Davis, carries Pierce's disease resistance from Vitis arizonica bred into a predominantly vinifera white wine grape.

directions: Caminante Blanc was released in late 2019 as the fifth of UC Davis's Pierce's disease-resistant wine grapes, bred by Dr. Andy Walker with resistance from Vitis arizonica introgressed into a mostly Vitis vinifera vine. The wine shows characteristics of both Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay, giving growers in high-disease-pressure areas a vinifera-quality white option that can survive where traditional varieties fail. Gulf South and Texas vineyards contending with severe glassy-winged sharpshooter and Pierce's disease pressure are among those beginning to plant it. Train on a cordon trellis in full sun; because it is a recent, patent-pending release, nursery stock remains limited.
sources: UC Davis College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences

common_name: Miss Blue Grape (USDA/Mississippi-Bred Pierce's Disease-Prone-Region Bunch Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant rooted vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; released from the same USDA breeding program at Meridian, Mississippi that produced the Pierce's disease-tolerant Miss Blanc and MidSouth bunch grapes.

directions: Miss Blue was developed by USDA researcher N.H. Loomis at the Meridian, Mississippi field station alongside the sister releases Miss Blanc and MidSouth, both bred specifically for the Deep South's severe Pierce's disease pressure. The dark-blue berries form in open, well-aerated clusters and are recommended for juice and jelly rather than fresh eating, typically ripening from late July into mid-August. Unlike Pierce's disease, anthracnose is the main disease concern for this variety, so a regular fungicide program is needed to keep the fruit clean. Grow on a sturdy trellis in full sun with good air circulation, and prune hard each winter to renewal spurs to maintain fruit quality.

common_name: Ramsey Grape Rootstock (Salt Creek, Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Nematode-Resistant Understock)

planting.note: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then bench-graft or field-bud a desired bunch grape variety onto the young rootstock; also sold as Salt Creek, valued in Texas and the Gulf South for its deep, drought-tolerant root system and tolerance of both Pierce's disease and root-knot nematodes.

directions: Ramsey, also marketed as Salt Creek, is a Vitis champinii rootstock selection, from the same tough native Texas species behind the Dog Ridge and Tampa rootstocks already grown across the Gulf South. Its deep, vigorous root system gives grafted vines strong drought tolerance and the ability to perform in poor, sandy, or high-pH caliche soils, while its champinii parentage confers useful field tolerance to Pierce's disease and strong resistance to root-knot nematodes. Growers bench-graft or bud a named bunch grape cultivar onto young Ramsey rootstock rather than growing it for its own fruit, which is small, seedy, and of no culinary interest. It is one of the standard rootstock choices in hot, humid, nematode- and Pierce's disease-prone vineyard sites in Texas and the wider Gulf Coast.
